title: The Samaritan Woman and the Official's Son
summary: Traveling through Samaria, Jesus rests at Jacob's well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. Their conversation moves from well water to living water, from her marital history to the true worship of the Father in spirit and truth, and Jesus tells her plainly that he is the Messiah. She tells her town, many Samaritans believe, and they call him the Savior of the world. Back in Cana, Jesus heals a royal official's dying son at a distance with a word, his second sign.
story:
Jesus has been in Judea, where his disciples baptized more people than John, and now he returns to Galilee by way of Samaria. Chapter 3 showed a respected Jewish teacher who came at night and struggled to understand. Chapter 4 shows a Samaritan woman, an outsider in every way a Jewish teacher would notice, who meets Jesus at noon and becomes a witness to her whole town. The contrast is deliberate: a named man and an unnamed woman, a ruler of the Jews and a villager of a despised people, a conversation that fades into silence and one that ends in a harvest. The good news moves beyond Jerusalem's boundaries, anticipating the mission of Acts 1:8 to Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth, and Acts 8 will tell of Philip's preaching and many believing in a city of Samaria.

The chapter closes with a royal official from Capernaum who believes Jesus' word without seeing, and whose son is healed at a distance. That story is numbered as the second sign and set, like the first, at Cana, so chapters 2 to 4 form a section that runs from Cana to Cana. Across that section Jesus has met a family at a wedding, the authorities at the temple, a Pharisee by night, a Samaritan woman and her town, and a royal official, and each meeting has shown a different kind of response: faith that grows, faith that is thin, faith that hesitates, faith that spreads, and faith that takes Jesus at his word. Chapter 5 will bring the first open hostility, and the tone of the Gospel will darken.
historical:
Jesus leaves Judea because the Pharisees have heard that he is making and baptizing more disciples than John (verses 1 to 3). The direct road from Judea to Galilee ran north along the central ridge through Samaria. Josephus says that Galileans customarily passed through Samaritan territory on their way to the festivals in Jerusalem (Antiquities 20.118), that by this route Jerusalem could be reached from Galilee in three days (Life 269), and that around AD 50 Samaritans at the border village of Ginae attacked a party of Galilean pilgrims and killed several, which set off a bloody feud (Antiquities 20.118-136). Some Jews took the longer road down the Jordan valley; Luke tells of a Samaritan village refusing to receive Jesus because he was heading for Jerusalem (Luke 9:52-53). John says Jesus ‘had to’ pass through Samaria (verse 4), using the same word, dei, that elsewhere in John marks divine necessity (3:7, 3:14, 3:30).

The Samaritans lived in the hill country between Judea and Galilee, centered on Shechem and Mount Gerizim. The Jewish account of their origins is 2 Kings 17: after Assyria took Samaria in 722 BC, it deported many Israelites and resettled the land with peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath, and elsewhere, of whom it says, “They worshiped the LORD, but they also served their own gods” (2 Kings 17:33). Josephus, following this account, often calls them Cutheans. The Samaritans understood themselves as descendants of the northern tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh and as the faithful keepers (shamerim) of the Law of Moses. Tension grew after the exile, when the returning Judeans refused their help in building the temple (Ezra 4:1-3). The Samaritans had their own sanctuary on Mount Gerizim, where Moses had commanded the blessing to be pronounced (Deuteronomy 11:29, 27:12). Josephus dates its building to the time of Alexander the Great (Antiquities 11.310-311, 11.322-324), but Yitzhak Magen's excavations on the mountain from 1983 onward found a sacred precinct going back to the fifth century BC. The Jewish high priest and ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed the temple and the city on Gerizim (Antiquities 13.254-256); coins from the destruction point to about 111 or 110 BC. The Samaritans continued to regard the mountain as the chosen place of worship, which is why the woman says, “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain” (verse 20).

Relations in Jesus' own lifetime were bitter. Josephus reports that during the governorship of Coponius (AD 6 to 9) some Samaritans slipped into the Jerusalem temple at Passover and scattered human bones in its porticoes, defiling it (Antiquities 18.29-30), and that in AD 36 a Samaritan prophet gathered crowds to ascend Gerizim, promising to show them sacred vessels buried there by Moses, until Pontius Pilate's troops attacked them; the complaint that followed led to Pilate's recall (Antiquities 18.85-89). The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses as Scripture, in their own form of the text, the Samaritan Pentateuch. Its most famous difference is at Deuteronomy 27:4, where it reads Mount Gerizim as the place for the altar where the Masoretic Text reads Mount Ebal, and it adds to the Ten Commandments a command to build the altar on Gerizim. Their hope centered on a coming figure based on the prophet like Moses of Deuteronomy 18:15-18, later called the Taheb, the Restorer, known from the fourth-century Samaritan teacher Marqah. A small Samaritan community survives today, around 900 people in 2024, living at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim and in Holon near Tel Aviv, and it still sacrifices the Passover lambs on the mountain.

Sychar (verse 5) was near ancient Shechem; it is usually identified with the village of Askar, about half a mile north of Jacob's well, though the Old Syriac version reads Shechem itself, and Tell Balata, the mound of Shechem, lies close by. Genesis records that Jacob bought land at Shechem (Genesis 33:19), that he gave Joseph “the ridge of land” (Genesis 48:22, where the Hebrew word shekem, ‘shoulder’ or ‘ridge’, plays on the town's name), and that Joseph's bones were buried there (Joshua 24:32). The Old Testament never mentions a well of Jacob, but a deep well at the foot of Mount Gerizim has been venerated as Jacob's well since at least the fourth century; Jerome mentions a church built over it, and a Greek Orthodox church, begun in the twentieth century on the plan of the Crusader church, was completed over the well in 2007. The royal official of verses 46 to 54 was basilikos, ‘a king's man’, probably an officer in the service of Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee and whom people popularly called king (Mark 6:14). Cana, in the hills north of Nazareth, lies a long day's walk from Capernaum on the lake, some sixteen to twenty miles depending on which site is Cana (see chapter 2), which is why the father met his servants on the road the next day.
cultural:
Drawing water was women's work, usually done in the cool of the morning or evening; Genesis speaks of evening as “the time when the women went out to draw water” (Genesis 24:11). The woman comes at the sixth hour, about noon if John counts hours from sunrise as Jews did. Many preachers have said she came at midday to avoid other women because of her reputation, but the text does not say so; travelers rested at midday, people drew water when they needed it, and the hour also sets her meeting in full daylight in contrast with Nicodemus's night.

Jesus crosses two social lines at once. First, Jewish teachers were wary of speaking with women in public; the Mishnah preserves the saying of Yose ben Yohanan of Jerusalem, one of the early sages, not to talk much with a woman (m. Avot 1:5), and the disciples' surprise in verse 27 reflects that caution. Second, Jews regarded Samaritans as unclean. Rabbi Eliezer is remembered as saying that one who eats the bread of Samaritans is like one who eats pork (m. Sheviit 8:10), and the Mishnah treats Samaritan women as menstruants from the cradle, and so a source of impurity (m. Niddah 4:1). David Daube (Journal of Biblical Literature 69, 1950) argued that the narrator's note in verse 9 means not merely that Jews do not associate with Samaritans but that they do not use vessels in common with them, which is exactly what Jesus proposes when he asks to drink from her jar. Sirach, a Jewish wisdom book of about 180 BC, calls the people who live at Shechem foolish (Sirach 50:25-26), a measure of how deep the contempt ran.

Living water was an everyday phrase for flowing water from a spring or stream, as opposed to the still water of a cistern, and the Law required it for some purifications (Leviticus 14:5, Numbers 19:17). The prophets used it for God himself: the Lord calls himself “the fountain of living water” forsaken for broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13, 17:13), and Zechariah promised that “living water will flow out from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 14:8). Isaiah invited the thirsty to come to the waters (Isaiah 55:1) and promised to pour water on thirsty land and his Spirit on Israel's descendants (Isaiah 44:3). John will later identify the living water with the Spirit (7:37-39).

Marriage and divorce also stand behind the conversation. Under the Law of Moses only a husband could initiate divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1-4), and in Jewish practice a wife could at most petition a court to compel her husband to release her. A woman with five former husbands had been widowed or divorced, or both, five times, and the man she now has is not her husband (verse 18). The text does not tell us how this came about, and the hard question below sets out the readings. The harvest sayings draw on farming life. In the land of Israel grain was sown in late autumn and reaped in spring, roughly four to six months later, so ‘four months until harvest’ sounds like a proverb for waiting. Jesus says the waiting is over, echoing Amos's picture of a time when “the plowman will overtake the reaper” (Amos 9:13). The saying “One sows and another reaps” (verse 37) turns a proverb of loss (compare Micah 6:15, “You will sow but not reap”) into one of shared joy.
literary:
The conversation at the well is one of the longest dialogues in the Gospels, and it follows John's pattern of misunderstanding and revelation. She hears living water as flowing well water; Jesus means the gift of God that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. A second misunderstanding follows with the disciples about food (verses 31 to 34), parallel to the first about water. Her names for Jesus climb as the conversation goes on: a Jew (verse 9), Sir (kurie, which can also mean Lord, verses 11, 15, 19), a prophet (verse 19), perhaps the Christ (verse 29), and finally, from her townspeople, the Savior of the world (verse 42). Jesus' self-revelation in verse 26, “I who speak to you am He”, is literally ‘I am, the one speaking to you’ (egō eimi), the first of many such sayings in John and an echo of God's self-naming in Isaiah (Isaiah 43:10, 52:6 in the Greek).

The scene also echoes the Old Testament's betrothal scenes at a well, which Robert Alter (The Art of Biblical Narrative, 1981) identified as a recurring type-scene: a man traveling in a foreign land meets a young woman at a well, one of them draws water, she runs home with the news, and the stranger is brought in and given hospitality, leading to marriage (Abraham's servant and Rebekah, Genesis 24; Jacob and Rachel, Genesis 29; Moses and Zipporah, Exodus 2:15-21). John's scene has the foreign land, the well, the woman, the request for water, the running home, and the invitation to stay, but no marriage; instead the talk of husbands becomes a talk about true worship, and the Baptist has just called Jesus the bridegroom (3:29). Many modern readers have seen the bridegroom gathering a people to himself here. Details are carefully placed. The woman leaves her water jar (verse 28), a small sign that she has found other water. The disciples wonder but do not ask (verse 27). The Samaritans come out across the fields as Jesus speaks of fields white for harvest (verses 30 and 35).

The closing healing (verses 46 to 54) is told in a pattern John has used before at Cana: a request, an apparent rebuff (verse 48, where ‘you people’ is plural), a persistent plea, and a word that exceeds the request. The official's faith grows in steps: he asks Jesus to come (verse 47), he believes Jesus' word and goes (verse 50), and when he learns the hour, he and his whole household believe (verse 53). The word hour frames the ending, from the seventh hour when the fever left to the recognition that it was the very hour Jesus spoke. The section from 2:1 to 4:54 closes with its own inclusio: Cana, the first sign, and the second sign.

outline.t: Jesus travels through Samaria to Jacob's well
Worship in spirit and truth; I am He
The woman's witness; the fields ripe for harvest
The Samaritans believe: the Savior of the world
The official's son healed, the second sign

doctrines.note: “A time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (verse 23). True worship is no longer tied to Gerizim or Jerusalem; it is directed to the Father, enabled by the Spirit, and shaped by the truth revealed in Jesus, the new temple (2:21). And the initiative is God's: the Father is seeking such worshipers.

“God is Spirit” (verse 24) does not mean that God is one spirit among many (the KJV's ‘God is a Spirit’ can mislead) but that he is not bound to a place, a body, or a mountain. Because of what God is, worship must correspond to him, in spirit and in truth, rather than to our geography.

Jesus reveals himself as the Messiah more directly to this Samaritan woman than to anyone else in John (verses 25-26). He is the prophet who knows her life, the giver of living water, and, in the Samaritans' own confession, “the Savior of the world” (verse 42), not only of Israel.

The chapter shows the gospel crossing ethnic, religious, and gender boundaries. Jesus' food is to finish the Father's work (verse 34), the fields are already ripe (verse 35), and a Samaritan woman becomes the first person in John's Gospel to bring a whole community to him. The disciples reap where others have labored (verse 38).

The chapter traces faith growing in stages. The Samaritans believe first because of the woman's word and then “because of His message” (verse 41), coming to know for themselves. The official believes Jesus' word before he sees (verse 50) and then believes with his whole household when the word is confirmed (verse 53).

words.note: Proskuneō, to worship, originally to bow down or prostrate oneself before someone as a sign of reverence. It occurs 60 times in the New Testament, 11 times in John, nine of them in verses 20 to 24, and 24 times in Revelation. BDAG gives its basic sense as expressing deep respect by bowing or kneeling, used of homage to rulers as well as worship of God. Its concentration here shows that the conversation's real subject is worship: the question is no longer where to bow down, but how, and to whom.

Alētheia, truth. It occurs 109 times in the New Testament, 25 times in John and nine in 1 John. In ordinary Greek it meant what is real as opposed to what merely appears; in the Hebrew Scriptures the corresponding word (emet) stresses reliability and faithfulness. In John it gathers both: the reality of God revealed in Jesus, who is full of grace and truth (1:14) and later says he is the truth (14:6). To worship in truth is to worship God as he really is and has made himself known, and it is paired here with spirit, not set against it.

Pēgē, spring, fountain. It occurs 11 times in the New Testament, three of them in this chapter and five in Revelation (where God gives from the spring of the water of life, Revelation 21:6). John varies his words for the well: the narrator calls it a pēgē, a spring-fed well (verse 6), while the woman calls it a phrear, a dug well or shaft (verses 11 and 12). Jesus picks up pēgē for the spring he gives, which wells up within a person to eternal life (verse 14): not water hauled up with effort, but a source that rises of itself.

Dōrea, gift, free gift. It occurs 11 times in the New Testament, only here in John. In Acts and Paul it names God's free gift, most often the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38, 8:20, 10:45) or the gift of righteousness in Christ (Romans 5:15-17). “If you knew the gift of God” (verse 10) sets the whole conversation on the footing of grace: Jesus begins by asking for a drink, but what he offers cannot be earned or drawn, only asked for and received.

Messias, Messiah. The Greek transliteration of the Aramaic meshiḥa, ‘anointed one’, occurs only twice in the Bible, both in John (1:41, 4:25), and both times the narrator translates it as Christos. That a Samaritan woman uses it is striking, since later Samaritan sources speak rather of the Taheb, the Restorer; she may be using a Jewish term for a Jewish visitor, or John may be rendering her hope in the word his readers knew. Either way, Jesus accepts the title outright, as he does nowhere else so early in John.

Sōtēr, savior, deliverer. It occurs 24 times in the New Testament, once in John (verse 42), and the full phrase Savior of the world recurs only in 1 John 4:14. In the Greek Old Testament it is used of God (Isaiah 45:15, 45:21). In the Roman world it was an honorific for gods and rulers, and Craig Koester (Journal of Biblical Literature 109, 1990) showed that it was used of emperors from Julius Caesar to Hadrian. On the lips of Samaritans living under Rome, in a region whose chief city had been refounded as Sebaste in honor of Augustus, it is a confession that the true deliverer of the world is this Jewish teacher.

Therizō, to reap, harvest. It occurs 21 times in the New Testament, four of them in verses 36 to 38 and nowhere else in John. The prophets used harvest for the day of the Lord, both as judgment (Joel 3:13) and as joy (Psalm 126:5-6, Isaiah 9:3), and Jesus uses it in the Synoptic Gospels for the gathering of people into the kingdom (Matthew 9:37-38). Here the harvest is already under way as the Samaritans walk out to him, and sower and reaper rejoice together.

Zaō, to live. It occurs 140 times in the New Testament and 17 times in John, five of them in this chapter. It first qualifies the water: living water (verses 10 and 11). Then it becomes the word of healing: “Your son will live” (verse 50), repeated by the servants (verse 51) and by the narrator (verse 53). The same Jesus who gives the water of life gives a dying boy his life back, and the word life ties the two halves of the chapter together.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as fully human and more than a man. He is tired and thirsty and sits at a well at noon (verse 6), the only place in John where he is said to be weary, and he asks a stranger for a drink. Yet he is the one who gives living water, eternal life, to all who ask, and the one who knows a stranger's life without being told. The woman recognizes a prophet, and the Samaritans' hope for a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:18) stands behind her words. He declares himself the Messiah with the words ‘I am’, which in Isaiah God uses to name himself (Isaiah 43:10), and he is confessed as the Savior of the world, a title the Old Testament gives to God (Isaiah 45:21).

He also fulfills the promises of living water. The Lord had called himself the fountain of living water (Jeremiah 2:13), Isaiah had promised water on the thirsty land and the Spirit on Israel's children (Isaiah 44:3), and Zechariah and Ezekiel had seen living water flowing from Jerusalem's temple (Zechariah 14:8, Ezekiel 47:1-12). John later says that Jesus spoke of the Spirit, “whom those who believed in Him were later to receive” (7:39), and at the cross water flows from Jesus' side (19:34). The one who asks for a drink at Jacob's well is the source of the water the prophets promised, and he will say “I am thirsty” once more on the cross (19:28).

He is the fulfillment of the temple as well. Salvation is from the Jews (verse 22), and Jesus is himself a Jew, the one in whom Israel's hope arrives; yet the hour is coming when worship will belong to neither Gerizim nor Jerusalem, because the new temple is his own body (2:21). His food is to do the will of the one who sent him and to finish (teleiōsō) his work (verse 34), language he will use at the Last Supper, “by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do” (17:4), and that culminates in his cry from the cross, “It is finished” (19:30), from the same family of words. In Cana, his word alone gives life to a dying boy many miles away, a foretaste of the Son who gives life to whom he wishes (5:21) and whose voice the dead will hear (5:25).
interpretation:
The Samaritan woman is the subject of the earliest known commentary on any Gospel text. Heracleon, a disciple of the Gnostic teacher Valentinus, wrote on John around AD 170, and Origen preserved and answered much of his treatment of this chapter in book 13 of his Commentary on John (written in the 230s). Heracleon read the woman as a spiritual soul whose true husband was her heavenly counterpart; Origen, while rejecting his system, also read the story spiritually, as a soul moving from Jacob's well of Scripture read according to the letter to the living water of its spiritual sense. John Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch around 390 (Homilies on John 32 to 35), praised the woman's persistence and her eagerness to share her news. Augustine (Tractate on John 15) noted that some read the five husbands as the five books of Moses, and himself read them as the five senses that had ruled her before she came to reason and to Christ; he treated the official in Tractate 16.

The Eastern churches remember her by name as Photini (or Photina, ‘enlightened one’) and keep the fifth Sunday of Pascha (counting Easter Day as the first) as the Sunday of the Samaritan Woman. Later tradition, which historians regard as legend rather than record, says that she preached in Carthage and was martyred in Rome under Nero with her sons and sisters. In the West the Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman lectionary read verses 5 to 42 on the third Sunday in Lent in Year A, and in the Catholic rite of Christian initiation the passage accompanies the first of the scrutinies for those preparing for baptism at Easter. Duccio's panel Christ and the Samaritan Woman (1310-1311), from the predella of his Maestà for Siena Cathedral and now in the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid, shows Jesus seated on the well's rim, the woman with a jar on her head, and the disciples at the town gate. Horatius Bonar's hymn I Heard the Voice of Jesus Say (1846) gave English-speaking congregations the image of Jesus freely giving living water to the thirsty.

Modern readers have opened the story in several directions. David Daube (1950) argued that verse 9 concerns sharing vessels, and so purity law. Robert Alter (1981) identified the betrothal type-scene, and many commentators have followed him. Raymond Brown (The Community of the Beloved Disciple, 1979) proposed that Samaritan converts, with their hope for a prophet like Moses, joined the community behind John's Gospel and helped shape its high Christology, a hypothesis that remains debated. Craig Koester (1990) set the confession ‘Savior of the world’ against imperial usage. Feminist interpreters such as Sandra Schneiders (The Revelatory Text, 1991) read the woman as a theological partner and apostle to her town and the five husbands as a symbol of Samaria's divided covenant history, while social historians such as Lynn Cohick (Women in the World of the Earliest Christians, 2009) argued that repeated widowhood and divorce were common and that the text does not present her as immoral. The official's story has been compared since antiquity with the healing of the centurion's servant in Matthew 8:5-13 and Luke 7:1-10, a question taken up among the hard questions below.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles come from manuscripts. In verse 1 the manuscripts divide between ‘Jesus knew’ and ‘the Lord knew’: P66 in its first hand and Codex Sinaiticus read ‘Jesus’, which the current Nestle-Aland edition prints, while P75, a correction in P66, Codex Vaticanus, and most later manuscripts read ‘the Lord’, which the King James Version follows. The sentence is awkward either way, since it names Jesus again later in the verse. In verse 9 the narrator's explanation, “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans”, is missing from the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, from Codex Bezae, and from several Old Latin manuscripts, but most editors keep it as original. In verse 5 the Old Syriac version reads Shechem instead of Sychar, and Jerome in some works treated Sychar as a scribal corruption of Shechem, though most scholars now distinguish the village from the ancient city.

Other differences are matters of translation and punctuation. The verb in verse 9 (sunchrōntai) can mean ‘associate with’ (BSB, NIV) or ‘have dealings with’ (KJV, ESV), or, on Daube's reading, ‘use vessels in common with’. In verse 24 the KJV's ‘God is a Spirit’ has become ‘God is spirit’ or ‘God is Spirit’ in modern versions, since Greek has no indefinite article and the sense is God's nature, not his membership in a class. In verses 35 and 36 the word ēdē, ‘already’, can end verse 35 (‘they are white already to harvest’, KJV) or begin verse 36 (‘Already the reaper draws his wages’, BSB, following the Nestle-Aland punctuation). The hours in verses 6 and 52 are rendered literally as the sixth and seventh hour (KJV, ESV) or converted to noon and one in the afternoon (NIV), which assumes John counts from sunrise; B. F. Westcott argued that John counts from midnight, as Romans did for legal purposes, which would make them six o'clock and seven o'clock, but most commentators take the Jewish reckoning.

teach.big: Jesus, the weary Jew at Jacob's well, crosses every barrier to give the living water of God's Spirit to an outsider, reveals himself as Messiah and Savior of the world, and calls for worship that answers to God as he truly is, in spirit and in truth.

outline.t: The divine ‘must’ leads Jesus through hostile territory, and the eternal Word sits down tired: he meets people as a real man, in real heat, on their ground.
Jesus begins by asking, not lecturing, and turns a request for water into the offer of God's gift: the thirst he addresses is deeper than the one she named.
Jesus knows the whole truth of a person's life and speaks it without contempt; being fully known by him is the beginning of being helped.
The old argument about where to worship is answered by who is worshiped and how: in spirit and in truth, through the Messiah who is speaking.
A changed person becomes a witness at once, with a simple, honest testimony: come and see.
Jesus' deepest nourishment is doing the Father's will, and the harvest is ripe now; every believer reaps where others sowed, so no one owns the work.
Faith that begins with someone's testimony must become firsthand: we have heard for ourselves.
Jesus' word is enough: faith takes him at his word before seeing, and grows when the word proves true.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misreading turns the woman into a notorious sinner whom Jesus exposes, and preaches the story as a morality tale about her past. The text is more restrained: Jesus names her history but never calls her a sinner or commands repentance, and she becomes the first evangelist of her town. Whatever her past, the point is that Jesus knows her fully and still offers her living water. A second misreading uses ‘in spirit and in truth’ to set inner sincerity against outward forms, as if Jesus were rejecting ordered worship, sacraments, or gathered congregations; the contrast is between worship bound to a holy mountain and worship shaped by the Spirit and by the truth revealed in Jesus. A third makes ‘salvation is from the Jews’ either a slur on the Samaritans or a slogan against Judaism; it affirms that God's saving purpose came through Israel and arrives in a Jewish Messiah.

Teachers should also avoid reducing the harvest sayings to a program for evangelistic technique, or reading verse 38 as permission for one generation to despise the labor of the last. Avoid turning the betrothal echoes into romance; the scene uses marriage imagery for God and his people, not for Jesus and this woman. With the official, avoid teaching that stronger faith guarantees healing; the father's faith is small and even rebuked before it is honored, and the story's emphasis is on Jesus' word, not on the quality of the man's believing.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on anyone whose history of marriage, divorce, or widowhood has made them the subject of gossip, and on those who have been shamed in church for a past they could not control. Teach it with care: the text does not say why the woman had five husbands, and many women in her world were widowed or discarded through no fault of their own. Jesus' knowledge of her life leads not to exposure but to an offer. It will also touch those who feel like outsiders to the church because of ethnicity, class, or history, and those who are weary; Jesus himself sat down tired. The official's story will press on parents with sick or dying children. Honor the father's desperation, avoid promising that faith will always bring the healing asked for, and let the story's weight fall where John puts it: on a Lord whose word has authority over life and death, and who meets a frightened father on the road.

hard.q: Was the Samaritan woman notoriously immoral, as she is often portrayed?
hard.a:
The traditional reading is strong and widely held. Five husbands and a present partner who is not her husband (verse 18) look like a pattern of sexual sin, and Jesus' request to call her husband seems designed to bring it to light. On this reading, which runs through much medieval, Reformation, and modern evangelical preaching, her coming at noon suggests social exclusion, her change of subject to worship (verse 20) is an evasion, and her testimony, “He told me everything I ever did” (verse 39), is the relief of a sinner fully known and not rejected. Defenders note that Jesus elsewhere confronts sin directly (5:14, 8:11) and that the story's power depends on grace meeting real guilt.

Other readers find the text more restrained. Lynn Cohick (Women in the World of the Earliest Christians, 2009) argued that in the first century women married young and were often widowed, that divorce was in the husband's hands (Deuteronomy 24:1), and that a woman might be passed through several marriages for reasons not her own, as the Sadducees' question about seven brothers imagines (Luke 20:27-33); the man she now has might be a relative who supports her or a partner in an arrangement she could not formalize. Jesus does not call her a sinner or command her to repent, she engages him as a theological conversation partner, and her townspeople listen to her and come out, which is odd if she were a pariah. A third reading takes the five husbands symbolically. Augustine reports that some in his day read them as the five books of Moses; Sandra Schneiders (1991) and others read them as the foreign gods of the peoples resettled in Samaria in 2 Kings 17:24-41 (though that chapter names more than five) or as Samaria's divided covenant loyalty, which would make the exchange a prophetic word to Samaria rather than an exposure of one woman.

The text does not settle the question, and a teacher should not claim more than it says. What it does say is clear: Jesus knows her whole life, speaks of it without contempt, offers her living water, reveals himself to her as Messiah, and makes her the means by which her town comes to him.

hard.q: Is the Samaritan scene historical, or does it reflect the later church's mission to Samaria?
hard.a:
Critical scholars have raised serious questions. Samaritan messianic hope is known mainly from later sources: the figure of the Taheb, the Restorer, appears in Samaritan writings from the fourth century onward, such as those of Marqah, so a Samaritan woman speaking of the Messiah ‘called Christ’ may reflect Jewish or Christian vocabulary. The title ‘Savior of the world’ was, as Craig Koester (1990) showed, an imperial honorific, and it appears again only in 1 John 4:14, which suggests the language of the Johannine churches. Raymond Brown (The Community of the Beloved Disciple, 1979) proposed that the chapter reflects the entry of Samaritan converts into John's community, and Matthew 10:5 has Jesus forbid his disciples to enter any town of the Samaritans, while Acts 8 presents the Samaritan mission as something new after Pentecost. On such views the scene is a theological narrative shaped by later experience, whatever its roots.

Others defend its historical core. Josephus shows that Galilean pilgrims regularly passed through Samaria (Antiquities 20.118) and that a Samaritan prophet in AD 36 could gather crowds on Gerizim with a promise tied to Moses (Antiquities 18.85-87), which fits a first-century hope for a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:18) even before the later term Taheb. The chapter's local details, Sychar, Jacob's field, a deep well at the foot of the mountain, the dispute over Gerizim, are accurate. The woman's word is explicitly translated by the narrator (verse 25), and John elsewhere puts his own vocabulary on the lips of speakers without claiming a transcript. Luke also shows Jesus in contact with Samaritans (Luke 9:52-56, 10:30-37, 17:11-19), and Acts 8 describes Samaritans already open to the message. Commentators such as D. A. Carson (1991) and Craig Keener (The Gospel of John, 2003) hold that John has shaped a real encounter for his readers, while others treat the story as largely the evangelist's composition.

The question turns partly on how one judges John's Gospel as a whole, which is discussed in the introduction. Readers of different convictions can agree on what the scene means in John: the gospel reaches beyond Israel, through a Jewish Messiah, to a people Jews despised, and it does so through the testimony of a woman.
